analysis.one_liner: Requires hotels and short-term rentals to show the full price, including mandatory fees, in every advertised rate.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 384-25 in June 2024, but the Senate never voted on it before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required hotels, motels, inns, and short-term rentals — and the websites that list them — to advertise the total price of a stay, including every mandatory fee, instead of luring customers with a low base rate and adding resort or cleaning fees at checkout. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce the rule [S2][S3]. It also sets a single national standard, barring states from keeping their own advertising rules that differ from the federal one [S4]. The House passed it 384-25, but the Senate never brought it to a vote before the term ended [S6][S7].
analysis.who_benefits: Travelers booking hotels, motels, inns, and short-term rentals would see the true total price up front, including resort fees, cleaning fees, and other mandatory charges, instead of discovering them at checkout. Honest providers that already display full prices would compete on a level field with those using teaser rates.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Travelers booking lodging online or by phone

how_it_helps.text: Hotels, motels, inns, short-term rentals, and booking websites could no longer advertise a reservation price that leaves out mandatory fees; the full price would have to be shown up front [S2][S4]. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce the rule [S2][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Lodging providers and booking platforms would have to change how they advertise and could no longer attract customers with a base rate that omits mandatory fees. The bill would also override differing state advertising rules, taking that power from state regulators.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hotels, short-term rentals, and booking sites

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state and local laws that regulate how lodging prices are advertised, so states could not enforce their own stricter rules, and state lawsuits must pause while a federal case against the same defendant is pending [S4].
The definition of a mandatory fee excludes taxes and fees imposed by governments or government-created districts, so those charges could still be left out of the advertised total [S4].
Bookings made through corporate, government, or institutional travel programs are exempt from the requirement [S2][S4].
The rule would only apply to reservations made a year or more after enactment, and it does not apply retroactively to existing bookings [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: travelers comparing rooms would see the true price up front, including resort and cleaning fees, instead of discovering them at checkout [S2][S3]. The main drawbacks are the fine print: the bill preempts state advertising rules that differ from the federal standard and pauses state lawsuits once the federal government sues [S4], its "mandatory fee" definition leaves out taxes and government-imposed fees [S4], it exempts corporate and government travel bookings [S2], and it would not take effect until a year after enactment [S4]. On balance a genuine consumer win, though weaker than the toughest state laws it would displace.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House by a wide margin, but the Senate referred it to its Commerce Committee, which never acted, so it died when the term ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 1, 2023, and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee [S6].
The committee approved it unanimously, 43-0, and reported it to the House floor in May 2024 [S6].
On June 11, 2024, the House passed it 384-25 under a suspension-of-the-rules procedure, which requires a two-thirds majority and allows no amendments [S6][S7].

The Senate received the bill on June 12, 2024, and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, where no further action was taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S6][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lodging operators and booking platforms are better off: they can keep advertising teaser prices and adding mandatory fees later, and no national or stricter state standard took effect.

sides.party_line_note: Passage was overwhelmingly bipartisan — 204 of 213 voting Democrats and 180 of 217 voting Republicans voted yes; all 25 no votes came from Republicans [S7].

industries.industry: Hotels, motels, and short-term rental operators
industries.note: They would have to show mandatory fees like resort fees in the advertised price instead of adding them at checkout [S4]. In exchange, the bill gives them one national advertising standard and overrides differing state rules [S4].

industries.industry: Online booking platforms and travel sites
industries.note: The bill covers websites and metasearch platforms that advertise lodging prices, so they too would have to show total mandatory fees up front [S4]. The national standard also replaces a patchwork of state rules they would otherwise have to track.

industries.industry: State attorneys general and state regulators
industries.note: States lose the ability to enforce their own lodging advertising rules that differ from the federal standard, and must pause state suits when the federal government files one against the same defendant [S4].
